opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a great example, because opening a cardboard box is exactly the kind of task where the trade-off gets interesting.

My background is mostly in simulation. With legged locomotion we showed you can train in a massively parallel simulator, thousands of robots at once, collect years of experience in minutes, and transfer that policy to the real robot with domain randomization. That works really well for locomotion because the hard part is the robot's own dynamics: rigid bodies, contacts with fairly simple terrain. Simulators model that reasonably well, and where they don't, you randomize enough that the policy becomes robust to the gap.

A cardboard box is a very different beast. You have deformable material, flaps that bend and spring back, tape that sticks and tears, friction that changes depending on how worn the cardboard is. Simulating all of that accurately is really hard, and simulating it fast enough to get the huge sample counts RL needs is even harder. So the sim-to-real gap is no longer something you can just randomize away. You'd be randomizing over physics you're not even modeling correctly in the first place.

On the other hand, real-world RL has its own problems. It's slow, you need resets, someone has to keep feeding the robot new boxes, the hardware wears out, and you have to worry about safety while the policy is still exploring. You're never going to get billions of samples in the real world.

So I'd think about it as a combination. Use simulation for what it's good at: the robot's own kinematics and dynamics, rough reaching and grasping behaviors, maybe a simplified box model so the policy learns the general structure of the task. Then bring in real data, through fine-tuning with real-world RL, demonstrations, or learning a better model of the box from real interactions, to close the gap on the parts simulation just can't capture.

In general I'd say the more the task depends on the robot itself, the more you can lean on simulation, and the more it depends on complicated interactions with the environment, the more real data you need. Box opening sits pretty far toward the second end, so I wouldn't rely on simulation alone. I still wouldn't throw it away, though, because the scale it gives you is too valuable.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we think about a lot, because a cardboard box is actually a really nice example of where the two approaches pull in different directions.

For locomotion, which is where I've spent most of my time, simulation is almost a solved question. The physics of a rigid robot walking on terrain is something we can model well, we can randomize over friction and mass and motor properties, and we can train in massively parallel environments and get policies that transfer quite reliably. So there, I'd basically never argue for doing the bulk of learning on the real robot.

A cardboard box is different. It's deformable, the flaps bend and crease in ways that are genuinely hard to simulate accurately, there's tape, there's friction between the fingers and the cardboard that depends on things like how worn the surface is. And the task is contact-rich in a way that walking isn't. Every bit of the interesting behavior happens exactly where the simulator is least trustworthy. So if you train purely in sim, you tend to get a policy that has learned to exploit whatever your deformable model does, and then it does something strange on the real box.

That said, I don't think the answer is to throw out simulation. The way I'd weigh it is: use simulation for everything it's good at, which is the structure of the behavior. Reaching, coarse positioning, recovering when the box slides, coordinating two arms or a hand and the body. You can learn all of that in sim with a crude box model, and you can afford to be very aggressive with domain randomization so the policy doesn't trust the fine details. Then the part that depends on the actual material properties, how hard to press, how to get a finger under a flap, you want to fine-tune or at least calibrate on the real system, with a relatively small amount of data.

The argument against doing a lot of real-world RL is simply cost. Every sample is wall-clock time, the robot wears, you destroy boxes, and if you're doing exploration with a real robot in contact with the world you need safety constraints that limit how much it can actually try. So you want the real-world phase to be about correcting a policy that's already mostly right, not discovering the behavior from scratch.

One thing I'd add is that the gap is shrinking from the simulation side too. Simulators are getting better at deformables, and more importantly we're getting better at learning the parts we can't model, so you can have a learned residual on top of the physics and keep most of the training in sim. My honest expectation is that in a few years, even for tasks like this, the real-world component ends up being mostly system identification and a bit of adaptation rather than real reinforcement learning in the traditional sense.

astra-6.text:
I think the main trade-off is how difficult the interaction is to simulate versus how expensive it is to collect experience on the real robot. With a cardboard box, the contact and deformation matter a lot. If your simulator doesn’t capture those well, a policy can learn something that works in simulation but doesn’t transfer to the real box.

On the other hand, reinforcement learning on the real robot means you have to keep resetting the task. Once you’ve opened or damaged the box, somebody has to prepare it again. That can become a bigger bottleneck than the learning algorithm itself.

So I would look at a combination: use simulation to learn what it can represent reliably, then use real-world experience to address the remaining gap. The important test is whether simulation actually reduces the amount of real-world interaction you need to get a reliable result.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main trade-off is how much interaction you need and how accurately you can simulate the task. With a cardboard box, the contact and deformation are quite complicated. You can build a simulation, but the policy might learn to exploit details of that simulation that don’t hold on the real robot.

Training directly in the real world avoids that gap, but now you have to collect all those interactions, reset the box after each attempt, and make sure the robot can explore safely. So I’d look for a combination: use simulation to learn the broad behavior, then use real-world data to adapt and validate it. The question is whether building a sufficiently useful simulation saves you more effort than collecting the data directly.
